title: Neural Modal Decomposition: Architectural Priors from Observables
claim: Direct regression needs a separate model per port count; ours learns shared pole-residue structure once and generalizes zero-shot to any port count.
layout: 3 panels: (a) top, (b) bottom-left vs (c) bottom-right, flow left-to-right
description: The top panel (a) shows a green 3D resonator blob with arrows for ports 1 to N. A large arrow leads to three boxes labeled RF/Microwave, Photonic devices and Quantum chips. Each box holds its own pole-residue equation. A bracket merges the three into a boxed 'Universal architectural prior' equation, H_ij = sum_k l_{k,i} r_{k,j} / (jω − p_k), with the terms colored red, blue and green. The bottom row has two panels. Panel (b), 'Direct regression', stacks 2-port, 3-port and N-port resonators. Each has a growing S-matrix and arrows to its own surrogate model box. Panel (c), 'Neural Modal Decomposition' in red, is a pipeline. It runs from the 2-port S matrix through an S→Z transform and training to poles and couplings. These are reconstructed into Z, then used for zero-shot N-port Z, then converted back to S. The eye goes first to the large titles and the colored equations.
caption: A shared architectural prior across physical domains, and comparison between direct regression and NMD. (a) Multi-port LTI systems in RF/microwave engineering, photonic devices, and superconducting quantum chips share the pole-residue form. (b) Direct regression on $S$-parameters needs a separate dataset and model for each port count $N$. (c) NMD converts the 2-port $S$ training data to the impedance $Z$, which keeps the same poles when ports are added or removed (Section [ref]), learns $p_k$ and the per-port couplings $l_{k,i}, r_{k,j}$, and assembles $Z$ for any $N$ ports zero-shot before converting back to $S$.
abstract: Many engineering building blocks behave as multi-port linear time-invariant systems. RF cavities, photonic devices, and superconducting quantum chips, despite their different underlying physics, all share a common mathematical structure for their port-level response. Each entry of the response matrix is a sum of contributions from a small number of intrinsic resonant modes, the pole-residue form. A model capable of predicting such responses for arbitrary geometries and arbitrary port configurations, while simultaneously extracting the underlying eigenmode structure, could therefore offer a design principle potentially applicable across all these domains. We propose a neural framework that learns this modal decomposition end-to-end, supervised only by system-level observables and without supervising the modal parameters themselves. The architecture decomposes into a port-independent pole predictor and two port-dependent coupling predictors whose outputs are combined entry-wise, separating intrinsic from port-dependent features. This factorization yields a single trained model that generalizes to port counts unseen during training, whereas direct regression needs a separate model for each port count, with an output size that grows as $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$. Although the modal parameters are never supervised, the freely parameterized poles converge to the physical resonances, in agreement with poles extracted by the AAA rational approximation algorithm. We instantiate the framework in radio-frequency electromagnetic surrogate modeling. A model trained only on 2-port data accurately predicts $N$-port responses unseen during training.
